claim: The mammalian genome encodes nine protein arginine methyltransferases (PRMTs 1–9).
source: The mammalian genome encodes nine protein arginine methyltransferases (PRMTs 1–9; PRMT4 is also known as CARM1).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the number of PRMTs encoded in the mammalian genome.

claim: PRMT4 is also known as CARM1.
source: The mammalian genome encodes nine protein arginine methyltransferases (PRMTs 1–9; PRMT4 is also known as CARM1).
evidence: This is an established nomenclature fact about PRMT4.

claim: Arginine methylation is critical in regulating signal transduction, gene expression, and splicing.
source: Arginine methylation is critical in regulating signal transduction, gene expression, and splicing (reviewed by Guccione and Richard, 2019; Lorton and Shechter, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: PRMT5 and its cofactors pICln and MEP50 (also known as WDR77) are important for assembly of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs).
source: For instance, an important function of PRMT5 and its cofactors pICln and MEP50 (also known as WDR77) is assembly of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs)—core components of the spliceosome (Meister et al., 2001; Neuenkirchen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: snRNPs are core components of the spliceosome.
source: For instance, an important function of PRMT5 and its cofactors pICln and MEP50 (also known as WDR77) is assembly of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs)—core components of the spliceosome (Meister et al., 2001; Neuenkirchen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of snRNPs in splicing.

claim: PRMT5/pICln provides non-enzymatic chaperoning of Sm proteins following their translation.
source: This includes both non-enzymatic chaperoning of Sm proteins via PRMT5/pICln following their translation and post-translational methylation of SmD1 (SNRPD1), SmD3 (SNRPD3), and SmB/B′ (SNRPB), by PRMT5-MEP50 (Friesen et al., 2001; Meister et al., 2001; Paknia et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: PRMT5-MEP50 catalyzes post-translational methylation of SmD1 (SNRPD1), SmD3 (SNRPD3), and SmB/B′ (SNRPB).
source: This includes both non-enzymatic chaperoning of Sm proteins via PRMT5/pICln following their translation and post-translational methylation of SmD1 (SNRPD1), SmD3 (SNRPD3), and SmB/B′ (SNRPB), by PRMT5-MEP50 (Friesen et al., 2001; Meister et al., 2001; Paknia et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Following methylation, Sm proteins are delivered to the Survival of Motor Neuron (SMN) assembly factor.
source: Following their methylation, these Sm proteins are delivered to the Survival of Motor Neuron (SMN) assembly factor, by which they are bound to small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs) in preparation for further processing and eventual nuclear import (Boisvert et al., 2002; Meister and Fischer, 2002; Pellizzoni et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: SMN binds Sm proteins to small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs) in preparation for further processing and eventual nuclear import.
source: Following their methylation, these Sm proteins are delivered to the Survival of Motor Neuron (SMN) assembly factor, by which they are bound to small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs) in preparation for further processing and eventual nuclear import (Boisvert et al., 2002; Meister and Fischer, 2002; Pellizzoni et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Disruption of PRMT5 leads to numerous splicing defects, primarily exon skipping (SE) and intron retention (RI).
source: Disruption of PRMT5 leads to numerous splicing defects, primarily exon skipping (SE) and intron retention (RI) (Boisvert et al., 2002; Bezzi et al., 2013; Koh et al., 2015; Braun et al., 2017; Fedoriw et al., 2019; Fong et al., 2019; Radzisheuskaya et al., 2019; Tan et al., 2019; Li et al., 2021; Sachamitr et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Intron retention is a highly prevalent alternative splicing event in tumors and is ubiquitous across cancer types.
source: Intron retention is a highly prevalent alternative splicing event in tumors and is ubiquitous across cancer types (Dvinge and Bradley, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: RNA splicing occurs either during transcriptional elongation or after the transcript has been cleaved and released from polymerase.
source: RNA splicing occurs either during transcriptional elongation or after the transcript has been cleaved and released from polymerase (reviewed by Neugebauer, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Whether PRMT5 exerts its influence over co- or post-transcriptional splicing is still unknown.
source: Although the importance of PRMT5 in preserving splicing integrity is clear, whether PRMT5 exerts its influence over co- or post-transcriptional splicing is still unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Previous work has indirectly implicated PRMT5 in the regulation of post-transcriptional splicing in Arabidopsis.
source: Previous work has indirectly implicated PRMT5 in the regulation of post-transcriptional splicing in Arabidopsis and also as a regulator of detained introns (DI)—a class of retained, unspliced introns in poly(A) RNA that remain nuclear and are removed prior to cytoplasmic export (Braun et al., 2017; Jia et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: PRMT5 has been implicated as a regulator of detained introns (DI).
source: Previous work has indirectly implicated PRMT5 in the regulation of post-transcriptional splicing in Arabidopsis and also as a regulator of detained introns (DI)—a class of retained, unspliced introns in poly(A) RNA that remain nuclear and are removed prior to cytoplasmic export (Braun et al., 2017; Jia et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Detained introns (DI) are a class of retained, unspliced introns in poly(A) RNA that remain nuclear and are removed prior to cytoplasmic export.
source: Previous work has indirectly implicated PRMT5 in the regulation of post-transcriptional splicing in Arabidopsis and also as a regulator of detained introns (DI)—a class of retained, unspliced introns in poly(A) RNA that remain nuclear and are removed prior to cytoplasmic export (Braun et al., 2017; Jia et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations.

claim: DI are highly conserved and enriched in RNA processing factor transcripts.
source: DI are highly conserved and enriched in RNA processing factor transcripts; their removal has been proposed as part of a feedback mechanism to control protein expression during differentiation and cell stress (Yap et al., 2012; Wong et al., 2013; Braunschweig et al., 2014; Boutz et al., 2015; Pimentel et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Removal of DI has been proposed as part of a feedback mechanism to control protein expression during differentiation and cell stress.
source: DI are highly conserved and enriched in RNA processing factor transcripts; their removal has been proposed as part of a feedback mechanism to control protein expression during differentiation and cell stress (Yap et al., 2012; Wong et al., 2013; Braunschweig et al., 2014; Boutz et al., 2015; Pimentel et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: PRMT5 inhibition leads to loss of Sm methylation and a simultaneous increase in DI.
source: As PRMT5 inhibition leads to loss of Sm methylation and a simultaneous increase in DI, Sm proteins have been implicated in regulating DI (Braun et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Sm proteins have been implicated in regulating DI.
source: As PRMT5 inhibition leads to loss of Sm methylation and a simultaneous increase in DI, Sm proteins have been implicated in regulating DI (Braun et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: A direct connection of DI or RI levels to Sm arginine methylation has not been established.
source: However, a direct connection of DI or RI levels to Sm arginine methylation has not been established.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The mechanistic role of Type I PRMTs (PRMT1–4, 6, and 8) in splicing is still poorly understood.
source: The mechanistic role of Type I PRMTs (PRMT1–4, 6, and 8) in splicing is still poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Type I PRMT inhibition leads to SE consequences.
source: Recent reports demonstrate that Type I PRMT inhibition leads to SE consequences (Fedoriw et al., 2019; Fong et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Many Type I-methylated proteins have a potential role in RNA post-transcriptional regulation.
source: Importantly, many of the Type I-methylated proteins have a potential role in RNA post-transcriptional regulation (Fedoriw et al., 2019; Fong et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: PRMT1 has been implicated in the regulation of RNA export through methylation of ALYREF and CHTOP.
source: Consistent with a role in post-transcriptional processing, the primary Type I methyltransferase, PRMT1, has been implicated in the regulation of RNA export; this regulation occurs through methylation of the Transcription and Export (TREX) components—Aly and REF export factor (ALYREF) and chromatin target of PRMT1 (CHTOP) (Hung et al., 2010; van Dijk et al., 2010; Chang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: PRMT1 is the primary Type I methyltransferase.
source: Consistent with a role in post-transcriptional processing, the primary Type I methyltransferase, PRMT1, has been implicated in the regulation of RNA export; this regulation occurs through methylation of the Transcription and Export (TREX) components—Aly and REF export factor (ALYREF) and chromatin target of PRMT1 (CHTOP) (Hung et al., 2010; van Dijk et al., 2010; Chang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PRMT1.

claim: Loss of CHTOP leads to an accumulation of nuclear polyadenylated transcripts, consistent with a block in RNA export.
source: Loss of CHTOP leads to an accumulation of nuclear polyadenylated transcripts, consistent with a block in RNA export (Chang et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: ALYREF and CHTOP are both deposited along nascent RNA and are also bound to RI.
source: Furthermore, ALYREF and CHTOP are both deposited along nascent RNA and are also bound to RI (Viphakone et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Nuclear export of RNA is intimately linked to splicing—dissociation of splicing factors is a prerequisite for successful export.
source: As the nuclear export of RNA is intimately linked to splicing—dissociation of splicing factors is a prerequisite for successful export—regulation of this process is a potential means to control RI (Luo and Reed, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The role of nuclear export factors and the impact of Type I PRMTs on regulating RI remains unexplored.
source: Despite this, the role of nuclear export factors and the impact of Type I PRMTs on regulating RI remains unexplored.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Both Type I and II PRMTs have been extensively reported to be required for the pathogenicity of lung cancer.
source: As both Type I and II PRMTs have been extensively reported to be required for the pathogenicity of lung cancer (Hwang et al., 2021)—yet their role in the transcription and splicing of this disease remains largely unstudied—we used A549 human alveolar adenocarcinoma cells as our model.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The role of Type I and II PRMTs in the transcription and splicing of lung cancer remains largely unstudied.
source: As both Type I and II PRMTs have been extensively reported to be required for the pathogenicity of lung cancer (Hwang et al., 2021)—yet their role in the transcription and splicing of this disease remains largely unstudied—we used A549 human alveolar adenocarcinoma cells as our model.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: GSK591 (also known as EPZ015866 or GSK3203591) is a potent and selective inhibitor of PRMT5.
source: Using GSK591 (also known as EPZ015866 or GSK3203591), a potent and selective inhibitor of PRMT5 (Duncan et al., 2016), and MS023, a potent pan-Type I inhibitor (Eram et al., 2016), we demonstrate that PRMTs inversely regulate RI post-transcriptionally through either Sm or CHTOP arginine methylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: MS023 is a potent pan-Type I inhibitor.
source: Using GSK591 (also known as EPZ015866 or GSK3203591), a potent and selective inhibitor of PRMT5 (Duncan et al., 2016), and MS023, a potent pan-Type I inhibitor (Eram et al., 2016), we demonstrate that PRMTs inversely regulate RI post-transcriptionally through either Sm or CHTOP arginine methylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: PRMTs inversely regulate RI post-transcriptionally through either Sm or CHTOP arginine methylation.
source: Using GSK591 (also known as EPZ015866 or GSK3203591), a potent and selective inhibitor of PRMT5 (Duncan et al., 2016), and MS023, a potent pan-Type I inhibitor (Eram et al., 2016), we demonstrate that PRMTs inversely regulate RI post-transcriptionally through either Sm or CHTOP arginine methylation.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: All PRMTs can generate monomethyl arginine (Rme1).
source: All PRMTs can generate monomethyl arginine (Rme1).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PRMT enzymatic activity.

claim: Type I PRMTs catalyze the formation of asymmetric NG,NG-dimethylarginine (Rme2a).
source: Type I PRMTs further catalyze the formation of asymmetric NG,NG-dimethylarginine (Rme2a); Type II PRMTs (PRMT5 and 9) form symmetric NG,N'G-dimethylarginine (Rme2s).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PRMT enzymatic activity.

claim: Type II PRMTs (PRMT5 and 9) form symmetric NG,N'G-dimethylarginine (Rme2s).
source: Type I PRMTs further catalyze the formation of asymmetric NG,NG-dimethylarginine (Rme2a); Type II PRMTs (PRMT5 and 9) form symmetric NG,N'G-dimethylarginine (Rme2s).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PRMT enzymatic activity.

claim: PRMT5 is the primary Type II methyltransferase.
source: PRMT5 is the primary Type II methyltransferase (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Significant differences in RI were observed with GSK591, MS023, and co-treatment with both inhibitors (FDR < 0.05) relative to DMSO.
source: Using replicate Multivariate Analysis of Transcript Splicing (rMATS) (Shen et al., 2014) to identify alternative splicing events, we observed significant differences in RI with GSK591, MS023, and co-treatment with both inhibitors (FDR < 0.05) relative to DMSO (Figure 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: RI were increased with GSK591 and co-treatment relative to DMSO.
source: Furthermore, whereas RI were increased with GSK591 and co-treatment—signified by a positive difference in percent spliced in (+ΔPSI or +ΔΨ)—RI were decreased with MS023 treatment (−ΔΨ) relative to DMSO.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: RI were decreased with MS023 treatment relative to DMSO.
source: Furthermore, whereas RI were increased with GSK591 and co-treatment—signified by a positive difference in percent spliced in (+ΔPSI or +ΔΨ)—RI were decreased with MS023 treatment (−ΔΨ) relative to DMSO.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There were 239 common introns between treatment conditions in A549 at day 2.
source: We next intersected all common RI between treatment conditions in A549 at day 2 (Figure 1c). We found 239 common introns.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: GSK591 and co-treatment with both inhibitors had increased inclusion for the 239 common introns, while MS023 treatment resulted in decreased inclusion relative to DMSO.
source: Strikingly, whereas GSK591 and co-treatment with both inhibitors had increased inclusion, for the same introns, MS023 treatment resulted in decreased inclusion relative to DMSO (Figure 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The median ΔΨ for the subset of 239 common introns did not significantly differ from the parent population.
source: When analyzing the distribution of ΔΨ for this subset of common introns (as in Figure 1b), the median ΔΨ did not significantly differ from the parent population (not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data analysis.

claim: The subset of 239 common RI is suitably representative of the larger group of PRMT-regulated RI.
source: This observation indicates that this subset of RI is suitably representative of the larger group of PRMT-regulated RI.
evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical analysis of the data.

claim: GAS5, ANKZF1, and NOP2 were identified by rMATS as containing inversely regulated RI after either Type I or II PRMT inhibition.
source: To confirm and quantify the presence of PRMT-regulated RI by RT-qPCR, we selected three representative genes, GAS5, ANKZF1, and NOP2. These were identified by rMATS as containing inversely regulated RI after either Type I or II PRMT inhibition (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The expression of GAS5 and NOP2 was increased with GSK591 treatment.
source: Notably, while the expression of GAS5 and NOP2 was increased with GSK591 treatment, it was unchanged with MS023 treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The expression of GAS5 and NOP2 was unchanged with MS023 treatment.
source: Notably, while the expression of GAS5 and NOP2 was increased with GSK591 treatment, it was unchanged with MS023 treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: GAS5 intron 9, ANKZF1 intron 9, and NOP2 intron 14 had increased retention upon GSK591 treatment (p=0.141, 0.016, and 0.001, respectively).
source: Consistent with our rMATS data, GAS5 intron 9, ANKZF1 intron 9, and NOP2 intron 14 had increased retention upon GSK591 treatment (p=0.141, 0.016, and 0.001, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RT-qPCR experimental data.

claim: GAS5 intron 9, ANKZF1 intron 9, and NOP2 intron 14 had less retention with MS023 treatment (p<0.0001, 0.064, and 0.040, respectively).
source: Furthermore, despite decreased dynamic range inherent to quantifying intronic signal loss, we observed less retention with MS023 treatment (p<0.0001, 0.064, and 0.040, respectively) (Figure 1e).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RT-qPCR experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Independent transduction of two unique guide RNAs (gRNA) for 4 days targeting PRMT1, PRMT4, or PRMT5 resulted in a robust reduction of their RNA expression.
source: Independent transduction of two unique guide RNAs (gRNA) for 4 days targeting either the major Type I methyltransferases—PRMT1 and PRMT4—or the Type II methyltransferase, PRMT5, resulted in a robust reduction of their RNA expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Knockdown of PRMT5 with both unique gRNAs recapitulated increased RI in GAS5 intron 9, ANKZF1 intron 9, and NOP2 intron 14.
source: Furthermore, we recapitulated increased RI in GAS5 intron 9, ANKZF1 intron 9, and NOP2 intron 14 by RT-qPCR following knockdown of PRMT5 with both unique gRNAs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RT-qPCR experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The stronger PRMT1 gRNA resulted in reduced RI in GAS5 intron 9 and ANKZF1 intron 9, but not NOP2 intron 14.
source: When analyzing RI following transduction with the stronger PRMT1 gRNA, we also observed reduced RI in GAS5 intron 9, ANKZF1 intron 9, but not NOP2 intron 14 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the RT-qPCR experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Knockdown of PRMT4 only reduced RI in GAS5 intron 9 with one gRNA, but not in ANKZF1 intron 9 or NOP2 intron 14.
source: Knockdown of PRMT4 only reduced RI in GAS5 intron 9 with one gRNA, but not in ANKZF1 intron 9 or NOP2 intron 14.
evidence: This claim is supported by the RT-qPCR experimental data.

claim: Treatment with GSK591 or MS023 resulted in a stronger decrease in total cellular dimethylarginine levels compared to PRMT knockdown.
source: Consistently, treatment with GSK591 or MS023 resulted in a stronger decrease in total cellular dimethylarginine levels, while PRMT knockdown only modestly decreased dimethylarginine, likely owing to incomplete depletion of the enzymes through this approach.
evidence: This claim is supported by the western blot data comparing inhibitor treatment to knockdown.

claim: PRMT knockdown only modestly decreased dimethylarginine, likely owing to incomplete depletion of the enzymes through this approach.
source: Consistently, treatment with GSK591 or MS023 resulted in a stronger decrease in total cellular dimethylarginine levels, while PRMT knockdown only modestly decreased dimethylarginine, likely owing to incomplete depletion of the enzymes through this approach.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of inhibitor treatment and knockdown effects.

claim: 2444 unique methylations across 585 proteins were identified in the A549 arginine methylome, the majority of which were involved in nuclear and chromatin regulation.
source: We recently published an extensive proteomic and transcriptomic characterization of the A549 arginine methylome in response to GSK591 and MS023 treatment (Maron et al., 2021). In that work, we identified 2444 unique methylations across 585 proteins, the majority of which were involved in nuclear and chromatin regulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' prior published work.

claim: MS023 treatment resulted in an increase in Rme1 and Rme2s in the chromatin fraction.
source: We observed the following changes: (1) an increase in Rme1 and Rme2s with MS023 treatment; (2) an increase in Rme2a with GSK591 treatment; (3) decreased Rme2s with GSK591 treatment; and (4) decreased Rme2a with MS023 treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by the western blot data of the chromatin fraction shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: GSK591 treatment resulted in an increase in Rme2a in the chromatin fraction.
source: We observed the following changes: (1) an increase in Rme1 and Rme2s with MS023 treatment; (2) an increase in Rme2a with GSK591 treatment; (3) decreased Rme2s with GSK591 treatment; and (4) decreased Rme2a with MS023 treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by the western blot data of the chromatin fraction shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: GSK591 treatment resulted in decreased Rme2s in the chromatin fraction.
source: We observed the following changes: (1) an increase in Rme1 and Rme2s with MS023 treatment; (2) an increase in Rme2a with GSK591 treatment; (3) decreased Rme2s with GSK591 treatment; and (4) decreased Rme2a with MS023 treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by the western blot data of the chromatin fraction shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: MS023 treatment resulted in decreased Rme2a in the chromatin fraction.
source: We observed the following changes: (1) an increase in Rme1 and Rme2s with MS023 treatment; (2) an increase in Rme2a with GSK591 treatment; (3) decreased Rme2s with GSK591 treatment; and (4) decreased Rme2a with MS023 treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by the western blot data of the chromatin fraction shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d.

claim: GSK591 and MS023 are specific and effective in depleting cellular methylarginine.
source: In addition to previously published reports using these same inhibitors, our data support that GSK591 and MS023 are specific and effective in depleting cellular methylarginine (Chan-Penebre et al., 2015; Duncan et al., 2016; Eram et al., 2016; Fong et al., 2019; Plotnikov et al., 2020; Maron et al., 2021; Sachamitr et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data in the manuscript and citations to prior research.

claim: The consequences of MS023 treatment on RI are likely more robust than the targeted CRISPR interference due to the ability of the remaining PRMTs to scavenge each other's substrates.
source: As MS023 inhibits multiple Type I enzymes, the consequences of MS023 treatment on RI are likely more robust than the targeted CRISPR interference due to the ability of the remaining PRMTs to scavenge each other's substrates (Dhar et al., 2013; Eram et al., 2016; Maron et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known properties of MS023 and PRMTs, supported by citations.

claim: There was a highly significant overlap in RI between all the data sets analyzed (Fisher's exact adjusted p<1e−05).
source: As demonstrated by the high odds ratio (log2(OR)>6) between all the data sets, we showed that there was a highly significant overlap in RI (Fisher's exact adjusted p<1e−05, Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2a.

claim: The high level of overlap between cell models and inhibition approaches establishes the importance of PRMTs in regulating RI.
source: This high level of overlap between cell models and inhibition approaches further establishes the importance of PRMTs in regulating RI and also supports that the observed changes in RI are on-target effects of the inhibitors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical analysis of the data.

claim: The observed changes in RI are on-target effects of the inhibitors.
source: This high level of overlap between cell models and inhibition approaches further establishes the importance of PRMTs in regulating RI and also supports that the observed changes in RI are on-target effects of the inhibitors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical analysis of the data.

claim: RI have been previously reported to have common characteristics such as being shorter in length, closer to transcription end site (TES), and having reduced splice site strength.
source: RI have previously been reported to have common characteristics such as being shorter in length, closer to transcription end site (TES), and having reduced splice site strength (Braunschweig et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The RI were significantly closer to the TES when compared to the genomic distribution of A549 expressed introns (p<2.2e−16).
source: We found that the RI were significantly closer to the TES and shorter when compared to the genomic distribution of A549 expressed introns (p<2.2e−16) (Figure 1f and g).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 1f.

claim: The RI were significantly shorter when compared to the genomic distribution of A549 expressed introns (p<2.2e−16).
source: We found that the RI were significantly closer to the TES and shorter when compared to the genomic distribution of A549 expressed introns (p<2.2e−16) (Figure 1f and g).
evidence: This claim is supported by the statistical analysis shown in Figure 1g.

claim: RI have a preference for guanine three nucleotides downstream of the 5′ splice site.
source: Moreover, in analyzing the probability of nucleotide distribution at the 5′ and 3′ splice sites, we noted both a preference for guanine three nucleotides downstream of the 5′ splice site and increased frequency of cytosine in the polypyrimidine tract (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b.

claim: RI have increased frequency of cytosine in the polypyrimidine tract.
source: Moreover, in analyzing the probability of nucleotide distribution at the 5′ and 3′ splice sites, we noted both a preference for guanine three nucleotides downstream of the 5′ splice site and increased frequency of cytosine in the polypyrimidine tract (Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the sequence analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b.

claim: The characteristics of RI (non-canonical splice sites, shorter length, and location closer to the TES) did not differ between the observed retained or removed introns.
source: Despite GSK591 and MS023 treatments' inverse effect on RI, these characteristics did not differ between the observed retained or removed introns.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of the data.

claim: GSK591 treatment did not significantly change the median of the genome-wide distribution of splicing rates compared to DMSO control (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p>0.05).
source: Surprisingly, compared to the DMSO control, GSK591 treatment did not significantly change the median of this distribution (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p>0.05), while MS023 treatment resulted in significantly slower global splicing rates (p<2.2e−16) (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the SKaTER-seq data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: MS023 treatment resulted in significantly slower global splicing rates (p<2.2e−16).
source: Surprisingly, compared to the DMSO control, GSK591 treatment did not significantly change the median of this distribution (Wilcoxon rank-sum test, p>0.05), while MS023 treatment resulted in significantly slower global splicing rates (p<2.2e−16) (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by the SKaTER-seq data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: There was no significant difference in the median splicing rate of introns that were retained with GSK591 treatment compared to DMSO (p=0.53).
source: We found no significant difference in the median of GSK591-treated cells compared to DMSO (p=0.53), while MS023 treatment led to slower splicing rates (p=0.07) (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the SKaTER-seq data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: MS023 treatment led to slower splicing rates for introns that were retained (p=0.07).
source: We found no significant difference in the median of GSK591-treated cells compared to DMSO (p=0.53), while MS023 treatment led to slower splicing rates (p=0.07) (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by the SKaTER-seq data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Changes in intron retention following PRMT inhibition were not entirely due to co-transcriptional splicing.
source: These observations therefore suggested that changes in intron retention following PRMT inhibition were not entirely due to co-transcriptional splicing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the SKaTER-seq data analysis.

claim: Introns that were retained in GSK591- or MS023-treated cells were slower to splice when compared to all introns (p=0.01 and p=0.17, respectively).
source: We observed that, when compared to all introns, introns that were retained in GSK591- or MS023-treated cells were slower to splice (p=0.01 and p=0.17, respectively) (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by the SKaTER-seq data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Analysis of RI in DMSO-treated cells revealed a significantly slower splicing rate (p=3.6e−6).
source: However, consistent with slower splicing as a general feature of RI, analysis of these same RI in DMSO-treated cells similarly revealed a significantly slower splicing rate (p=3.6e−6) (Figure 2d, left violin plots).
evidence: This claim is supported by the SKaTER-seq data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Introns located closer to the TES had slower splicing rates.
source: Indeed, we determined that introns located closer to the TES had slower splicing rates (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This claim is supported by the SKaTER-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: RI transcription was completed significantly faster in DMSO-, GSK591-, and MS023-treated cells (p=1.03e−24, 1.94e−15, and 3.00e−7, respectively).
